title: 你的 GPU 不是算力不足，而是 KV 缓存不够：PagedAttention 和 vLLM 如何解决 LLM 服务问题
author: M.T.Ramkrushna
content:
Tuesday Weekly AI Post, part two. This morning was about fine-tuning a model cheaply (LoRA and QLoRA). This afternoon is about the other half of the bill: serving it. Specifically, the piece of GPU memory that quietly decides how many users you can handle at once, the KV cache, and the idea that made vLLM fast: PagedAttention.

Short version: when you self-host an LLM, throughput is usually limited by memory, not math. And for a long time, serving systems wasted most of the memory they reserved for the KV cache.

What the KV cache is

LLMs generate one token at a time. For every new token, attention needs the keys and values of every previous token in the sequence. Recomputing them each step would be absurd, so servers keep them in GPU memory: the KV cache.

It has two properties that make it hard to manage:

  • It's large. The vLLM paper (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023) works through OPT-13B: one token's KV cache is 2 (key and value) × 5120 (hidden size) × 40 (layers) × 2 bytes (FP16) = 800 KB. At OPT's 2,048-token max length, one request can need up to 1.6 GB.
  • It's dynamic. You don't know in advance how long the output will be. It grows token by token and disappears when the request ends.

My own arithmetic for a more current model (not from the paper): Llama 3 8B has 32 layers and uses grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads of dimension 128. Per token that's 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes, about 128 KB. An 8,192-token context is then about 1 GiB of KV cache per sequence. Ten long concurrent chats and you've spent 10 GB before thinking about anything else. GQA helps a lot, but the cache still scales with users × context length.

Why older servers wasted it

Most deep learning frameworks want tensors in contiguous memory, so earlier serving systems stored each request's KV cache as one contiguous chunk, pre-allocated for the maximum possible length. That causes three kinds of waste:

  1. Reservation: space held for tokens that haven't been generated yet.
  2. Internal fragmentation: space reserved for a max length the request never reaches.
  3. External fragmentation: gaps between differently sized chunks that no new request fits into.

The paper's profiling found that in existing systems only 20.4%–38.2% of KV cache memory actually held token states. The vLLM launch blog puts it as 60%–80% of memory wasted to fragmentation and over-reservation.

Wasted cache memory means a smaller batch. A smaller batch means lower throughput on the same GPU.

PagedAttention: virtual memory for attention

The fix borrows an old operating-systems idea: paging.

PagedAttention splits each sequence's KV cache into fixed-size blocks, each holding the keys and values for a fixed number of tokens. Blocks don't need to be next to each other in GPU memory. A per-sequence block table maps logical blocks (positions in the sequence) to physical blocks (wherever they live), and the attention kernel fetches the blocks it needs.

What that buys you:

  • Allocate on demand. New physical blocks are allocated as tokens are generated, not reserved up front.
  • Waste only in the last block. The blog reports near-optimal usage, under 4% waste.
  • Sharing. Sequences can point at the same physical blocks.

That last one matters more than it sounds. With parallel sampling (n completions from one prompt) or beam search, the sequences share the prompt's blocks. vLLM uses reference counts and copy-on-write: a shared block is copied only when one sequence needs to write something different into it. The blog reports this cuts memory for these sampling methods by up to 55%, which can mean up to 2.2× throughput. The paper also discusses the same trick for a shared prefix, such as a long system prompt reused across requests.

When memory runs out anyway

Paging doesn't create memory. When the GPU fills up, vLLM preempts some sequences and either:

  • Swaps their blocks to CPU RAM, or
  • Recomputes their KV cache later. The paper notes this can be cheaper than it sounds: the already generated tokens are appended to the prompt and the whole thing is processed in one prompt-phase pass.

Which one wins depends on CPU-GPU bandwidth and GPU compute.

The results (and what they're compared against)

  • Paper: 2–4× throughput at the same level of latency versus FasterTransformer and Orca, with bigger gains for longer sequences, larger models and more complex decoding.
  • Launch blog (ShareGPT-style lengths): up to 24× higher throughput than Hugging Face Transformers and up to 3.5× higher than TGI. With one output per request: 14–24× vs HF and 2.2–2.5× vs TGI. With three parallel outputs: 8.5–15× vs HF and 3.3–3.5× vs TGI.

Read the baselines carefully. "24×" is against plain HF Transformers generation, not against a tuned modern server. These are 2023 numbers, and other servers have since adopted paged KV caches too. The durable lesson is the idea, not the multiplier.

What this means if you self-host

A minimal vLLM server: 

pip install vllm

vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
  --max-model-len 8192 \
  --enable-prefix-caching

And how I'd think about the knobs:

  1. Budget the KV cache per user, not just the weights. Do the per-token math for your model (layers × KV heads × head dim × 2 × bytes) and multiply by realistic context length and concurrency.
  2. Don't set max context higher than you need. A larger --max-model-len lets single requests eat more cache. Match it to your real traffic.
  3. Turn on prefix caching when prompts share a long prefix (same system prompt, same few-shot examples, same document). That's the shared-prefix case the paper describes.
  4. Use n > 1 sampling without fear of copying the prompt. Shared blocks plus copy-on-write make it much cheaper than separate requests.
  5. Measure the right things under real load: throughput (tokens/s), time to first token, inter-token latency, and how often requests get preempted. A benchmark with one user tells you nothing about batching.
  6. If you're memory bound, look at the cache before buying GPUs. Smaller KV (GQA models, KV cache quantization where your server supports it), shorter contexts, and better batching often beat more hardware.

The takeaway

For LLM serving, the scarce resource is often memory per concurrent sequence, and the KV cache is where it goes. PagedAttention's contribution was treating that memory the way an OS treats RAM: small pages, a lookup table, sharing, and copy-on-write. Everything else, the bigger batches and the throughput numbers, follows from not wasting it.

If you self-host: what limits you first, KV cache memory or compute?

aiSummary: 本文解释了在 LLM 服务中，限制吞吐量的瓶颈是 KV 缓存内存而非算力，并介绍 vLLM 的 PagedAttention 如何借鉴虚拟内存技术，将内存浪费从 60-80% 大幅降至 4% 以下，从而显著提升效率。
oneSentenceSummary: 本文解释了在 LLM 服务中，限制吞吐量的瓶颈是 KV 缓存内存而非算力，并介绍 vLLM 的 PagedAttention 如何借鉴虚拟内存技术，将内存浪费从 60-80% 大幅降至 4% 以下，从而显著提升效率。
summary: 本文探讨了 LLM 服务中的 KV 缓存瓶颈：内存管理效率低下会导致 60-80% 的 GPU 内存被浪费。文章介绍了 vLLM 的 PagedAttention 技术如何借鉴操作系统虚拟内存的概念——固定大小的块、块表和写时复制共享——相较于此前的系统实现 2-4x 的吞吐量提升。文章还为自托管提供实用建议，包括 KV 缓存内存预算、针对共享提示词进行前缀缓存，以及在真实负载条件下制定测量策略。

mainPoints.point: KV 缓存内存而非算力，是 LLM 服务的主要瓶颈
mainPoints.explanation: 对于 Llama 3 8B 这类模型，每个 token 约需要 128KB 的 KV 缓存。这意味着 10 段并发的长对话在尚未计入模型权重之前，就会占用 10GB 内存，因此内存管理对吞吐量至关重要。

mainPoints.point: 传统服务系统因过度预留和内存碎片，浪费了 60-80% 的 KV 缓存内存
mainPoints.explanation: 较早期的系统会为最大序列长度预先分配连续内存，导致预留浪费（未使用的空间）、内部碎片（分配过大的内存块）和外部碎片（不同内存分配之间的空隙）；实际用于存放 token 状态的内存仅占 20-38%。

mainPoints.point: PagedAttention 为注意力机制实现了操作系统式的虚拟内存
mainPoints.explanation: PagedAttention 将 KV 缓存拆分为固定大小的块，并通过每个序列的块表将逻辑位置映射到物理位置，从而按需分配内存，将浪费降至 4% 以下；它还支持在序列间共享内存块，并通过引用计数和写时复制实现管理。

mainPoints.point: 内存共享技术能够显著提升吞吐量
mainPoints.explanation: 并行采样和束搜索可以通过写时复制共享提示词块，将内存用量最多降低 55%，并将吞吐量最高提升至 2.2x；系统提示词中的共享前缀还能进一步提高效率。

mainPoints.point: 自托管的实用建议包括制定 KV 缓存预算和启用前缀缓存
mainPoints.explanation: 用户应计算每个 token 的 KV 缓存需求，根据实际流量设定 max-model-len，为共享提示词启用前缀缓存，并在真实负载下测量吞吐量、延迟和抢占率，而不是只依赖单用户基准测试。

keyQuotes: 自托管 LLM 时，吞吐量通常受内存限制，而非计算能力。
PagedAttention 会将每个序列的 KV 缓存拆分为固定大小的块，每个块存放固定数量 token 对应的键和值。
该博客称，内存利用率已接近最优，浪费低于 4%。
无服务器 GPU 是一种无需预先配置的 GPU：有任务到来时，平台会启动你的容器；容器运行期间计费；流量停止后则缩减至零。
对于 LLM 服务而言，稀缺资源往往是每个并发序列可用的内存，而 KV 缓存正是内存的主要去向。
